claim: CTCF binding has been previously shown to take place over large and phased nucleosomal arrays displaying a prominent NDR.
source: CTCF binding has been previously shown to take place over large and phased nucleosomal arrays displaying a prominent NDR (Fu et al., 2008; Teif et al., 2014; Barisic et al., 2019; Wiechens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: 52,129 CTCF binding regions were identified in ES cells cultured in serum and LIF.
source: We identified 52,129 regions displaying robust peaks that significantly overlap with previous studies (Nora et al., 2017; Davis et al., 2018; Pękowska et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq experimental data performed by the authors.

claim: The identified CTCF binding regions significantly overlap with previous studies.
source: We identified 52,129 regions displaying robust peaks that significantly overlap with previous studies (Nora et al., 2017; Davis et al., 2018; Pękowska et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published datasets and shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The aggregate of CTCF motifs directly correlates with CTCF occupancy.
source: At these regions, we observed that the aggregate of CTCF motifs directly correlates with CTCF occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the authors' ChIP-seq data and motif analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The presence of CTCF cognate binding sequence drives CTCF recruitment.
source: At these regions, we observed that the aggregate of CTCF motifs directly correlates with CTCF occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the presence of its cognate binding sequence drives CTCF recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between motif presence and CTCF occupancy observed in the data.

claim: At individual CTCF binding regions, highly organized nucleosome arrays are observed, particularly over large CTCF peaks.
source: At individual CTCF binding regions, we observed highly organized nucleosome arrays, particularly over large CTCF peaks (Figure 1A; bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase-seq and related nucleosome profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CTCF binding regions display a well defined NOA/NDR/NOA structure surrounding CTCF motifs.
source: We observed a very well defined NOA/NDR/NOA structure surrounding CTCF motifs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on V-plot analysis of MNase-seq data shown in figures.

claim: CTCF binding footprints were detected within the NDR except upon H3 ChIP.
source: CTCF binding footprints, identified as small MNase (<100 bp) and ATAC (<150 bp) fragments, were also detected within the NDR except upon H3 ChIP (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, and H3 ChIP-seq data shown in figures.

claim: CTCF binding at its motif is closely associated with nucleosome positioning.
source: These observations indicate that CTCF binding at its motif is closely associated with nucleosome positioning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed correlation between CTCF binding and nucleosome organization patterns.

claim: The aggregate of CTCF motifs is correlated with CTCF occupancy when CTCF binding regions are ranked by peak height.
source: After ranking CTCF binding regions by their peak height, we confirmed that the aggregate of CTCF motifs is correlated with CTCF occupancy (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq and motif data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: As the motif score and CTCF binding diminishes, the associated MNase- and ATAC-footprints decrease.
source: Further, as the motif score and CTCF binding diminishes, the associated MNase- and ATAC-footprints decrease (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MNase-seq and ATAC-seq footprinting data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The reduction of CTCF binding across regions correlates with a progressive loss of nucleosome order.
source: Notably, the reduction of CTCF binding across the regions correlates with a progressive loss of nucleosome order (Figure 2C), consistent with what has been previously observed (Vainshtein et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' MNase-seq data and is consistent with prior published observations.

claim: As CTCF binding decreases, the −1 and +1 nucleosomes roll inwards, shrinking the NDR and resulting in increased nucleosome occupancy at the CTCF motif.
source: This is particularly well illustrated by the quantitative analysis of the position of the −1 and +1 nucleosomes, which roll inwards, shrinking the NDR and resulting in increased nucleosome occupancy at the CTCF motif (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of nucleosome positioning data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The interaction of CTCF with its cognate motif acts as a major force driving the establishment of NDRs/NOAs.
source: These observations argue that the interaction of CTCF with its cognate motif acts as a major force driving the establishment of NDRs/NOAs, as previously suggested by siRNA knock-down of CTCF (Wiechens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' data and is supported by prior siRNA knockdown studies.

claim: CTCF-aid ES cells display reduced CTCF expression compared to wild-type cells.
source: In accord with the hypomorphic behavior of this line (Nora et al., 2017), CTCF-aid displayed reduced expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with prior characterization.

claim: CTCF-aid ES cells display reduced bulk chromatin association compared to wild-type cells.
source: In accord with the hypomorphic behavior of this line (Nora et al., 2017), CTCF-aid displayed reduced expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), bulk chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is based on chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CTCF-aid ES cells display reduced CTCF binding levels compared to wild-type cells.
source: In accord with the hypomorphic behavior of this line (Nora et al., 2017), CTCF-aid displayed reduced expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), bulk chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and binding levels (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Reduced CTCF binding in CTCF-aid cells correlates with less prominently positioned nucleosomes compared to wild-type cells.
source: In accord with the hypomorphic behavior of this line (Nora et al., 2017), CTCF-aid displayed reduced expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), bulk chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and binding levels (Figure 3A) that correlated with less prominently positioned nucleosomes compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon 2 hr IAA treatment, CTCF-aid expression is significantly reduced.
source: Upon a short (2 hr) treatment with the Auxin analog Indole-3-Acetic Acid (IAA), CTCF-aid expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and binding (Figure 3A) were significantly reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upon 2 hr IAA treatment, CTCF-aid chromatin association is significantly reduced.
source: Upon a short (2 hr) treatment with the Auxin analog Indole-3-Acetic Acid (IAA), CTCF-aid expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and binding (Figure 3A) were significantly reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon 2 hr IAA treatment, CTCF-aid binding is significantly reduced.
source: Upon a short (2 hr) treatment with the Auxin analog Indole-3-Acetic Acid (IAA), CTCF-aid expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and binding (Figure 3A) were significantly reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IAA-induced CTCF depletion leads to a dramatic loss of NOAs.
source: This led to a dramatic loss of NOAs, major displacements of the +/- 1 nucleosomes, and an invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: IAA-induced CTCF depletion leads to major displacements of the +/- 1 nucleosomes.
source: This led to a dramatic loss of NOAs, major displacements of the +/- 1 nucleosomes, and an invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: IAA-induced CTCF depletion leads to an invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes.
source: This led to a dramatic loss of NOAs, major displacements of the +/- 1 nucleosomes, and an invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The effect of CTCF depletion on nucleosome positioning was observed across different classes of functional genetic features.
source: Since this effect was observed across different classes of functional genetic features (Figure 3D), and rapidly follows loss of CTCF, we conclude that CTCF is a major determinant of local nucleosome positioning in steady-state conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MNase H3 ChIP-seq data at different genomic features shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CTCF is a major determinant of local nucleosome positioning in steady-state conditions.
source: Since this effect was observed across different classes of functional genetic features (Figure 3D), and rapidly follows loss of CTCF, we conclude that CTCF is a major determinant of local nucleosome positioning in steady-state conditions.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the rapid and widespread effects of CTCF depletion on nucleosome positioning.

claim: Proteomic approaches have identified CTCF on newly synthesized chromatin.
source: Given that proteomic approaches have identified CTCF on newly synthesized chromatin (Alabert et al., 2014), we aimed at studying the consequences of replication over CTCF binding sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior proteomic study.

claim: In Drosophila S2 cells, the reconstitution of specific NDRs/NOAs over active regulatory elements takes much longer than previously anticipated after replication.
source: In Drosophila S2 cells, the reconstitution of specific NDRs/NOAs over active regulatory elements, particularly at enhancers, takes much longer than previously anticipated (Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study in Drosophila S2 cells.

claim: In mouse ES cells, chromatin accessibility over TF binding sites is lost during replication and progressively reacquired as nascent chromatin matures.
source: Similarly, in mouse Embryonic Stem (ES) cells, chromatin accessibility over TF binding sites is lost during replication and progressively reacquired as nascent chromatin matures (Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study in mouse ES cells.

claim: CTCF binding regions display only minor changes, if any, immediately after replication.
source: Indeed, only minor changes, if any, were appreciable just after replication (Figure 4A; center panel).
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One hour after replication, CTCF binding regions acquire a nucleosomal structure indistinguishable from the controls.
source: During the following hour, CTCF binding regions acquire a nucleosomal structure indistinguishable from the controls (Figure 4A; right panel).
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CTCF is likely capable of rapidly rebinding its sites post-replication to efficiently re-establish NDRs and NOAs.
source: Given the direct role of CTCF in local nucleosome positioning (Figures 2 and 3), it is therefore likely that CTCF is capable of rapidly rebinding its sites post-replication to efficiently re-establish NDRs and NOAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rapid restoration of nucleosome positioning at CTCF sites after replication and CTCF's known role in nucleosome positioning.

claim: ES cell enhancers display an increase in nucleosome density over the NDRs and attenuated NOAs immediately after replication.
source: We observed an increase in nucleosome density over the NDRs and attenuated NOAs immediately after replication (Figure 4A; center panel), contrasting markedly with CTCF binding regions.
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data at p300-marked enhancers shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One hour after replication, ES cell enhancers are near completely restored.
source: One hour after replication, however, we observed that ES cell enhancers were near completely restored (Figure 4A; right panel)
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ES cells are more efficient than S2 cells in reconfiguring nucleosome positioning at enhancers after replication.
source: One hour after replication, however, we observed that ES cell enhancers were near completely restored (Figure 4A; right panel), indicating that ES cells are more efficient than S2 cells in reconfiguring nucleosome positioning at enhancers.
evidence: The claim is inferred by comparing the authors' ES cell data with prior S2 cell data.

claim: At regions bound by Oct4/Sox2, nucleosome positioning is altered upon replication.
source: At regions bound by Oct4/Sox2, nucleosome positioning was altered upon replication (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The pioneer activity of Oct4 and Sox2 is not sufficient to rapidly reorganize nucleosomal arrays after replication.
source: This indicates that the pioneer activity of these two factors (Soufi et al., 2015), illustrated here by the detection of a nucleosome overlapping their motif (Figure 4A), is not sufficient to rapidly reorganize nucleosomal arrays after replication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed alteration of nucleosome positioning at Oct4/Sox2 sites after replication, despite their known pioneer activity.

claim: Regions organized by Esrrb display a prominent NDR centered on the Esrrb motif, two particularly well positioned flanking nucleosomes and a persistent NOA, just after replication.
source: Regions organized by Esrrb, however, displayed a prominent NDR centered on the Esrrb motif, two particularly well positioned flanking nucleosomes and a persistent NOA, just after replication (Figure 4A; center panel).
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At Esrrb regions, the NDR and the positioning of the +/- 1 and surrounding nucleosomes are more prominent immediately after replication than after 1 hr.
source: Strikingly, the NDR and the positioning of the +/- 1 and surrounding nucleosomes were more prominent immediately after replication than after 1 hr (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Following replication, Esrrb is rapidly rebound at its sites and imposes strong nucleosome positioning, which is subsequently modified by the binding of additional TFs.
source: This suggests that following replication, Esrrb is rapidly rebound at these sites and imposes strong nucleosome positioning, which is subsequently modified by the binding of additional TFs – a phenomenon that we previously described when we compared Esrrb binding in interphase and mitosis (Festuccia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed nucleosome dynamics at Esrrb sites and is consistent with prior observations.

claim: Different sets of TF binding regions substantially differ in post-replication nucleosome dynamics.
source: These observations, together with the analysis of p300-centered enhancers and CTCF binding regions, suggest that different sets of regions substantially differ in post-replication nucleosome dynamics.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of post-replication nucleosome dynamics at different TF binding regions.

claim: p300-enhancers and Oct4/Sox2 regions display comparably delayed restoration of nucleosome positioning after replication.
source: Both measurements clearly revealed a comparably delayed restoration of nucleosome positioning at p300-enhancers and Oct4/Sox2 regions after replication.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis (R2 and spectral density) of MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Esrrb and CTCF display increasing capacity to reinstate NDRs/NOAs minutes after the passage of the replication fork.
source: In contrast, Esrrb and CTCF, display, in turn, increasing capacity to reinstate NDRs/NOAs minutes after the passage of the replication fork.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis (R2 and spectral density) of MINCE-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differential post-replication nucleosome dynamics among TF binding regions are independently supported by analysis of repli-ATAC data.
source: These differential post-replication nucleosome dynamics among TF binding regions are independently supported by our analysis of repli-ATAC data recently generated in ES cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a technique where chromatin accessibility is measured as chromatin matures after replication (Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of published repli-ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Esrrb has been shown to bind at sites preserving NDRs/NOAs during mitosis.
source: Given that both Esrrb and CTCF can re-establish nucleosome positioning following replication, we then turned our attention to mitosis, where Esrrb has already been shown to bind at sites preserving NDRs/NOAs (Festuccia et al., 2016; Festuccia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Esrrb.

claim: CTCF binding regions display the typical NDR/NOA structure in mitotic cells.
source: Using MNase-seq data, we observed the typical NDR/NOA structure at CTCF binding regions in mitotic cells (Figure 5A) obtained by nocodazole shake-off with >95% purity (Festuccia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase-seq data in mitotic cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CTCF acts as a mitotic bookmarking factor.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that CTCF acts as a mitotic bookmarking factor (Shen et al., 2015; Sekiya et al., 2017; Zhang, 2019; Burke et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed nucleosome structure at CTCF sites in mitosis and is supported by citations to prior studies on mitotic bookmarking.

claim: CTCF displays site-specific interactions in mitotic cells associated with ordered nucleosomal arrays.
source: Thus, we performed CTCF ChIP-seq and observed site-specific interactions in mitotic cells associated with ordered nucleosomal arrays (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on CTCF ChIP-seq and MNase-seq data in mitotic cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 29,539 CTCF binding sites (56.7%) are bookmarked in mitosis.
source: Using a generalized linear model, we identified 29,539 bookmarked sites (56.7%) and categorized them according to the relative sizes of interphase and mitosis peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of CTCF ChIP-seq data in interphase and mitosis.

claim: Cohesin is fully evicted from its targets in mitosis.
source: Cohesin, a recurrent partner of CTCF in interphase (Merkenschlager and Nora, 2016), was found fully evicted from its targets in mitosis (Warren et al., 2000; Waizenegger et al., 2000) (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is based on SMC1 ChIP-seq data in mitosis shown in figures and is supported by prior citations.

claim: Nearly all regions displaying robust enrichment for Cohesin in interphase are bookmarked by CTCF.
source: Notably, we observed that nearly all regions displaying robust enrichment for Cohesin in interphase are bookmarked by CTCF, even though Cohesin accumulation is not a prerequisite for CTCF bookmarking (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of CTCF and SMC1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Cohesin accumulation is not a prerequisite for CTCF bookmarking.
source: Notably, we observed that nearly all regions displaying robust enrichment for Cohesin in interphase are bookmarked by CTCF, even though Cohesin accumulation is not a prerequisite for CTCF bookmarking (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of CTCF and SMC1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The existence of high quality CTCF motifs is a better indicator of binding in mitosis than in interphase.
source: Moreover, the existence of high quality CTCF motifs appeared to be a better indicator of binding in mitosis than in interphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the conditions for CTCF binding are more stringent in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the relationship between motif scores and CTCF binding in interphase and mitosis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The conditions for CTCF binding are more stringent in mitosis than in interphase.
source: Moreover, the existence of high quality CTCF motifs appeared to be a better indicator of binding in mitosis than in interphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the conditions for CTCF binding are more stringent in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that high quality motifs are better predictors of mitotic binding.

claim: CTCF mitotic bookmarking activity in ES cells contradicts recent data in human somatic cells.
source: Our finding of CTCF bookmarking activity in ES cells contradicts recent data in human somatic cells (Oomen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim compares the authors' findings with a recent publication in human somatic cells.

claim: Mouse somatic cell lines (NIH3T3 and C2C12) show no or reduced evidence of mitotic bookmarking activity by CTCF.
source: However, our analyses in mouse somatic cell lines (NIH3T3 and C2C12) revealed no or reduced evidence of mitotic bookmarking activity by CTCF (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on CTCF ChIP-seq data in mitotic NIH3T3 and C2C12 cells shown in figures.

claim: CTCF can decorate mitotic chromosomes globally in cell lines and embryos.
source: Therefore, even though CTCF can decorate mitotic chromosomes globally, as revealed by microscopy in cell lines and embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), this is not necessarily translated into mitotic bookmarking capacity in every cell type.
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Global decoration of mitotic chromosomes by CTCF is not necessarily translated into mitotic bookmarking capacity in every cell type.
source: Therefore, even though CTCF can decorate mitotic chromosomes globally, as revealed by microscopy in cell lines and embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), this is not necessarily translated into mitotic bookmarking capacity in every cell type.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CTCF decorates mitotic chromosomes in multiple cell types but only shows bookmarking activity in ES cells.

claim: The progressive reduction of mitotic CTCF binding correlates with a gradual loss of NDRs and NOAs.
source: Examining the association between CTCF binding and nucleosome positioning in mitosis, and in complement to the analysis in interphase (Figure 2), we found that the progressive reduction of mitotic CTCF binding correlates with a gradual loss of NDRs and NOAs (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of CTCF ChIP-seq and MNase-seq data in mitosis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At CTCF binding regions that lose CTCF in mitosis, nucleosomes are less well positioned.
source: Moreover, when CTCF binding regions were split as bookmarked or lost in mitosis, we could confirm that the nucleosomes are less well positioned (Figure 6B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is based on MNase-seq data comparing bookmarked and lost CTCF sites in mitosis shown in figures.

claim: At CTCF binding regions that lose CTCF in mitosis, nucleosomes exhibit clear displacements toward the motif.
source: Moreover, when CTCF binding regions were split as bookmarked or lost in mitosis, we could confirm that the nucleosomes are less well positioned (Figure 6B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and exhibit clear displacements toward the motif (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of nucleosome positioning at lost CTCF sites shown in figures.

claim: CTCF is a mitotic bookmarking TF that preserves nucleosome order during mitosis.
source: Overall, this establishes that CTCF is a mitotic bookmarking TF that preserves nucleosome order during mitosis.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the observed maintenance of nucleosome order at CTCF bookmarked sites in mitosis.

claim: CTCF bookmarked regions present a strong displacement inwards of the +1 nucleosome (25 bp) compared to the −1 nucleosome (3 bp).
source: Nevertheless, even CTCF bookmarked regions presented a strong displacement inwards of the +1 nucleosome (25 bp for +1 versus 3 bp for −1 nucleosome; Figure 6A,D) and a more moderate shift of all following nucleosomes (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of nucleosome positioning at bookmarked CTCF sites shown in Figure 6A,D.

claim: The constraints imposed on nucleosomes by CTCF are slightly different in interphase and in mitosis.
source: This indicates that the constraints imposed on the nucleosomes by CTCF are slightly different in interphase and in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in nucleosome positioning at CTCF sites between interphase and mitosis.

claim: The repositioning of the +1 nucleosome at CTCF sites in mitosis cannot be solely explained by the mitotic loss of Cohesin.
source: Since in interphase CTCF sites that do not bind Cohesin do not show this repositioning of the +1 nucleosome (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), it cannot be solely explained by the mitotic loss of Cohesin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of nucleosome positioning at CTCF sites with and without Cohesin shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Additional factors influence nucleosome positioning at CTCF binding regions in either interphase or mitosis.
source: Additional factors therefore influence nucleosome positioning at CTCF binding regions in either interphase or mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Cohesin loss alone cannot explain nucleosome repositioning.

claim: The hypomorphic nature of CTCF-aid binding is amplified in mitosis.
source: We observed that the hypomorphic nature of CTCF-aid binding was amplified in mitosis; CTCF-aid was barely detectable in bulk mitotic chromatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and more specifically at regions binding CTCF in wild-type mitotic cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on chromatin fractionation and ChIP-seq data in mitotic CTCF-aid cells shown in figures.

claim: Global loss of mitotic bookmarking in CTCF-aid cells is associated with acquisition of nucleosomal properties characteristic of regions losing mitotic CTCF binding in wild-type cells.
source: This global loss of mitotic bookmarking was associated with the acquisition of nucleosomal properties characteristic of regions losing mitotic CTCF binding in wild-type cells: nucleosome positioning was strongly attenuated (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B); the NDRs were partially invaded by nucleosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C); nucleosomes, especially upstream of the motif, shifted inwards (~55 bp upstream versus 21 bp downstream; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data in mitotic CTCF-aid cells shown in figures.

claim: IAA treatment of CTCF-aid cells leads to further invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes in mitosis.
source: These changes in nucleosome positioning were only minimally increased upon IAA treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D), which leads to further invasion of the NDR by nucleosomes (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is based on MNase H3 ChIP-seq data in IAA-treated mitotic CTCF-aid cells shown in figures.

claim: CTCF behaves as a canonical bookmarking factor in ES cells and actively maintains nucleosome order.
source: We conclude, therefore, that CTCF behaves as a canonical bookmarking factor in ES cells and actively maintains nucleosome order, mirroring our previous data on Esrrb (Festuccia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is concluded from the mitotic CTCF binding and nucleosome positioning data, and is compared to prior Esrrb data.

claim: Genes displaying slow reactivation dynamics after mitosis (Clusters 1 and 2) do not show enrichment for CTCF binding.
source: We observed that the two clusters displaying slow reactivation dynamics (Clusters 1 and 2) did not show any enrichment for CTCF binding.
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher Exact test analysis of CTCF peak enrichment near genes in different reactivation clusters.

claim: Genes with faster post-mitotic reactivation dynamics (Clusters 3, 4 and 5) show significant CTCF enrichment.
source: Contrastingly, clusters with faster dynamics (Clusters 3, 4 and 5) showed significant CTCF enrichment.
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher Exact test analysis of CTCF peak enrichment near genes in different reactivation clusters.

claim: At genes with fast post-mitotic reactivation (Clusters 4 and 5), more proximal (<100 kb) CTCF bookmarked sites are specifically and prominently enriched.
source: While the enrichment at Cluster three was similarly low and distal for both bookmarked and lost CTCF sites, at Clusters 4 and 5 more proximal (<100 kb) CTCF bookmarked sites were specifically and prominently enriched.
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher Exact test analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cluster 5, which exhibits the fastest post-mitotic reactivation dynamics, is particularly enriched in CTCF bookmarked sites compared to regions losing CTCF binding in mitosis.
source: Cluster 5, which exhibits the fastest reactivation dynamics, was found to be particularly enriched in CTCF bookmarked sites compared to regions losing CTCF binding in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher Exact test analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CTCF binding is associated with faster reactivation dynamics after mitosis, with CTCF bookmarking displaying the most robust association with gene reactivation.
source: We conclude, therefore, that CTCF binding is associated with faster reactivation dynamics after mitosis, with CTCF bookmarking displaying the most robust association with gene reactivation.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the analysis of CTCF enrichment at genes with different post-mitotic reactivation dynamics.

claim: Only genes with rapid reacquisition of TSS accessibility after replication (Cluster 4) and genes where TSSs remain accessible immediately after replication (Cluster 5) show robust CTCF enrichment.
source: Notably, only Cluster 4, which displays rapid reacquisition of accessibility, and Cluster 5, where TSSs remain accessible immediately after replication, show robust enrichments (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher Exact test analysis of CTCF enrichment at genes with different post-replication accessibility dynamics shown in Figure 7D.

claim: After both replication and mitosis, the presence of CTCF binding sites correlates with the speed and efficiency of gene reactivation.
source: Therefore, both after replication and mitosis, the presence of CTCF binding sites correlates with the speed and efficiency of gene reactivation.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the analysis of CTCF enrichment at genes with different reactivation dynamics after both replication and mitosis.

claim: CTCF is continuously required to maintain NDRs/NOAs at its binding sites.
source: While the role of CTCF in nucleosome positioning has already been suggested using siRNA knock-down (Wiechens et al., 2016), our work provides definitive evidence to conclude that CTCF is continuously required to maintain NDRs/NOAs at its binding sites.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the authors' auxin-depletion experiments and is contrasted with prior siRNA studies.

claim: There is a predictive relationship between the number and quality of CTCF binding motifs, the level of CTCF occupancy, and the degree of nucleosome positioning.
source: First, we describe a predictive relationship between the number and quality of CTCF binding motifs, the level of CTCF occupancy, and the degree of nucleosome positioning.
evidence: The claim summarizes the authors' findings on the correlation between motifs, CTCF binding, and nucleosome positioning.

claim: Loss of nucleosome order occurs 2 hr after CTCF depletion using the auxin degradation system.
source: Second, we observe a loss of nucleosome order 2 hr only upon CTCF depletion using the auxin degradation system.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' auxin-depletion experiments.

claim: CTCF likely positions nucleosomes by acting as a barrier to the nucleosome sliding activity of the chromatin remodeler SNF2H.
source: Given previous results, it is likely that CTCF positions nucleosomes by acting as a barrier to the nucleosome sliding activity of the chromatin remodeler SNF2H (Barisic et al., 2019; Wiechens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' results and prior studies on CTCF and SNF2H.

claim: Site-specific loss of CTCF binding in mitosis occurs at regions with poor binding motifs and reduced/absent Cohesin recruitment in interphase.
source: Furthermore, we show that the site-specific loss of CTCF binding in mitosis, which occurs at regions with poor binding motifs and reduced/absent Cohesin recruitment in interphase, is associated with a comprehensive loss of nucleosome order.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of CTCF binding, motifs, Cohesin, and nucleosome positioning in mitosis.

claim: At regions preserving CTCF binding in mitosis, proper NDRs/NOAs are maintained.
source: Conversely, at regions preserving CTCF binding in mitosis, proper NDRs/NOAs are maintained
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' MNase-seq data at CTCF bookmarked sites in mitosis.

claim: The severely hypomorphic CTCF-aid lacks both CTCF binding and nucleosomal order at CTCF sites in mitosis.
source: Conversely, at regions preserving CTCF binding in mitosis, proper NDRs/NOAs are maintained; an observation which is underlined by the severely hypomorphic CTCF-aid which both lacks binding of CTCF and nucleosomal order at CTCF sites in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' ChIP-seq and MNase-seq data in mitotic CTCF-aid cells.

claim: CTCF plays a key role in maintaining local nucleosome order in interphasic and mitotic ES cells.
source: Hence, our data in interphasic and mitotic ES cells establish that CTCF plays a key role in maintaining local nucleosome order.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the authors' comprehensive analysis of CTCF and nucleosome positioning in interphase and mitosis.

claim: CTCF not only maintains NDRs/NOAs, but also contributes to their establishment after DNA replication.
source: In addition, our observations following DNA replication further indicate that CTCF not only maintains NDRs/NOAs, but also contributes to their establishment, as suggested by the rapid reinstatement of nucleosome positioning after the passage of the replication fork.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' MINCE-seq data showing rapid nucleosome restoration at CTCF sites after replication.

claim: The rapid nucleosome restoration at CTCF sites after replication is independently supported by analyses of post-replication chromatin accessibility in ES cells.
source: This is independently supported by our analyses of post-replication chromatin accessibility (Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019) in ES cells
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of published repli-ATAC-seq data.

claim: Previous observations link CTCF binding to reduced DNA polymerase processivity and increased mutation rates at CTCF sites.
source: This is independently supported by our analyses of post-replication chromatin accessibility (Stewart-Morgan et al., 2019) in ES cells and, notably, by previous observations linking CTCF binding to reduced DNA polymerase processivity and increased mutation rates at CTCF sites (Smith and Whitehouse, 2012; Reijns et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CTCF is a major determinant of local nucleosome order, which orchestrates the organization of NDRs/NOAs throughout the cell-cycle.
source: We conclude, therefore, that CTCF is a major determinant of local nucleosome order, which orchestrates the organization of NDRs/NOAs throughout the cell-cycle.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the authors' comprehensive analysis of CTCF and nucleosome positioning during interphase, replication, and mitosis.

claim: The direct and near instant dependence of nucleosome positioning on CTCF binding establishes the molecular basis for CTCF to build local chromatin resiliency.
source: The direct and near instant dependence of nucleosome positioning on CTCF binding that we have described here, establishes the molecular basis for CTCF to build local chromatin resiliency.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the authors' findings on the rapid effects of CTCF binding/loss on nucleosome positioning.

claim: Both CTCF and Esrrb, two zinc finger TFs, confer similar properties to their respective binding sites during replication and mitosis.
source: Together with previous work (Festuccia et al., 2019), it appears that both CTCF and Esrrb, two zinc finger TFs, confer similar properties to their respective binding sites during replication and mitosis.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the authors' current work on CTCF and prior work on Esrrb.

claim: The number and type of zinc fingers do not seem to represent the intrinsic feature underlying the post-replication and mitotic activity of CTCF and Esrrb.
source: Whilst CTCF comprises 10 C2H2-type and 1 C2HC-type zinc fingers (Klenova et al., 1993), Esrrb contains two C4-type zinc fingers – as is frequently observed by similar nuclear receptors (Gearhart et al., 2003). Hence, the number and type of zinc fingers do not seem to represent the intrinsic feature underlying the post-replication and mitotic activity of CTCF and Esrrb.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of zinc finger types in CTCF and Esrrb, supported by citations.

claim: Zinc finger TFs, which rapidly scan DNA for their motifs to engage in stable binding, may be particularly suited to maintain nucleosome positioning after replication and during mitosis.
source: It nevertheless remains possible that zinc finger TFs, which rapidly scan DNA for their motifs to engage in stable binding (Iwahara and Levy, 2013), are particularly suited to maintain nucleosome positioning after replication and during mitosis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on known properties of zinc finger TFs and the authors' observations.

claim: Other C2H2 zinc finger TFs have been suggested to organize nucleosomes, including Zelda and Phaser in Drosophila, and REST and YY1 in mammals.
source: Other C2H2 zinc finger TFs have been suggested to organize nucleosomes: in Drosophila, Zelda (McDaniel et al., 2019) and Phaser (Baldi et al., 2018); in mammals, REST and YY1 (Valouev et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Current data suggests that Zelda may act following replication but not during mitosis.
source: Whether these factors also organize nucleosomes during replication and mitosis requires further study; however, current data suggests that Zelda may act following replication (McDaniel et al., 2019) but not during mitosis (Dufourt et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of prior studies on Zelda.

claim: Properties in addition to intrinsic DNA binding domains may be important for TFs to mediate their function during replication and mitosis.
source: Properties in addition to their intrinsic DNA binding domains may thus be important for TFs to mediate their function during replication and mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that not all zinc finger TFs may function during replication and mitosis.

claim: C2H2 zinc-fingers are typically phosphorylated during mitosis, preventing their site-specific interactions.
source: Notably, C2H2 zinc-fingers are typically phosphorylated during mitosis, preventing their site-specific interactions (Dovat, 2002; Rizkallah et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on mitotic phosphorylation of zinc fingers.

claim: It is possible that either CTCF specifically, or C2H2 zinc fingers more generally, are not mitotically inactivated in ES cells.
source: Given our results, it is possible that either CTCF specifically, or C2H2 zinc fingers more generally, are not mitotically inactivated in ES cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' observation of CTCF mitotic bookmarking in ES cells.

claim: Not all mitotic bookmarking TFs are zinc finger proteins, as illustrated by FoxA1 and Tbp.
source: Moreover, not all mitotic bookmarking TFs (Festuccia et al., 2017a) are zinc finger proteins, as illustrated by FoxA1 (Caravaca et al., 2013) or Tbp (Teves et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on non-zinc finger mitotic bookmarking factors.

claim: Several studies have assessed the mitotic bookmarking capacity of CTCF with varying results.
source: Several studies have thus far assessed the mitotic bookmarking capacity of CTCF, with varying results (Shen et al., 2015; Sekiya et al., 2017; Oomen et al., 2019; Burke et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies with conflicting findings.

claim: CTCF binding in mitosis is cell type-specific.
source: Here, we show that CTCF binding in mitosis is cell type-specific, possibly reconciling these conflicting observations.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' observation of CTCF bookmarking in ES cells but not in somatic cell lines.

claim: The mitotic bookmarking activity of CTCF is a developmentally regulated phenomenon.
source: Moreover, this indicates that the mitotic bookmarking activity of CTCF is a developmentally regulated phenomenon, which may be mediated by differential mitotic phosphorylation, as discussed above.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cell type-specific nature of CTCF bookmarking and is speculated to involve phosphorylation.

claim: Recent results show CTCF is capable of mitotic bookmarking in an erythroblast cell line.
source: In support of developmental regulation, recent results have shown CTCF is capable of mitotic bookmarking in an erythroblast cell line (Zhang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Since Cohesin is lost during prophase and is required to assemble Topological Associating Domains, CTCF bookmarking may not lead to the mitotic maintenance of these structures.
source: Nevertheless, since Cohesin is lost during prophase (Nishiyama et al., 2013), and is required to assemble Topological Associating Domains, CTCF bookmarking may not lead to the mitotic maintenance of these structures, as recently shown (Zhang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known requirement of Cohesin for TAD formation and its loss in mitosis, supported by citations.

claim: Nucleosomes are reorganized rapidly post-replication in ES cells at regulatory elements as compared to other cell types.
source: Indeed, we show here that nucleosomes are reorganized rapidly post-replication in ES cells at regulatory elements as compared to other cell types (Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' MINCE-seq data compared to prior studies in other cell types.

claim: Different TFs exhibit drastic differences in their ability to reposition nucleosomes after replication.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis indicates that different TFs exhibit drastic differences in their ability to reposition nucleosomes, with CTCF and Esrrb exhibiting a particularly compelling capacity to restructure nucleosomal arrays within minutes of the passage of the replication fork.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' comparative analysis of post-replication nucleosome dynamics at different TF binding sites.

claim: CTCF and Esrrb exhibit a particularly compelling capacity to restructure nucleosomal arrays within minutes of the passage of the replication fork.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis indicates that different TFs exhibit drastic differences in their ability to reposition nucleosomes, with CTCF and Esrrb exhibiting a particularly compelling capacity to restructure nucleosomal arrays within minutes of the passage of the replication fork.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' MINCE-seq data.

claim: The mechanisms identified may contribute to the continuous maintenance and regulation of gene activity during successive cell divisions in ES cells.
source: Since ES cell self-renewal requires constant proliferation, the mechanisms that we have identified may contribute to the continuous maintenance and regulation of gene activity during successive cell divisions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the authors' findings and the known properties of ES cells.

claim: The globally fast reorganization of nucleosomes after replication, together with the particular capacity of CTCF and Esrrb to govern nucleosome positioning after replication and during mitosis, may facilitate the reassembly of regulatory complexes in nascent chromatin fibers and in daughter ES cells.
source: The globally fast reorganization of the nucleosomes after replication, together with the particular capacity of CTCF and Esrrb to govern nucleosome positioning after replication and during mitosis, may indeed facilitate the reassembly of regulatory complexes in nascent chromatin fibers and in daughter ES cells (Mirny, 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' findings and supported by a citation.

claim: The correlation between post-replication/mitosis gene reactivation speed and CTCF binding provides support for the hypothesis that CTCF facilitates regulatory complex reassembly.
source: While this hypothesis needs to be directly addressed, the correlation between post-replication/mitosis gene reactivation speed and CTCF binding, provides clear support.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of gene reactivation dynamics and CTCF enrichment.
